issues.title: A perspective on the mediator
issues.author: brentzundel
issues.body:
from Michael Richardson:

> I spent a few months bring a PoC digital wallet system online in 2023.
> (I was the cat herder)
> 
> This document uses the term "mediator" in a way that I do not recognize.
> My experience is that wallets need an associated (public, cloud) didcom/w3c
> mediator helper because they are not always online, don't stay at a fixed
> address, and even if the previous two not true, often have too limited
> battery to be able to defend against DoS attacks.
> 
> Here is a old, but useful diagram of what I mean:
>   https://github.com/Sirius-social/didcomm-mediator/blob/main/docs/Mediation.md
> 
> I can't tell if this document is talking about the same thing, but it does
> not seem so, as it seems to suggest that mediators would sometimes get access
> to the private part of the credential itself.
> 
> ---
> 
> I am very interested in the mediator role (as I think of it) because I think
> if done naively, it will lead to extreme centralization.
> Either to <5 BigTech operators, or to a single nation supplied mediator subject to
> surviellance and control. These are layer 8 and layer 9 considerations that we
> have to take into account at other layers.
> 
> The only time I can see a mediator not needed is when I present, in-person, my
> legal-age-to-drink credential via BTLE/QRcode to the bouncer at the line to
> enter the club.

issues.title: Non-linkability language adjustment
issues.author: brentzundel
issues.body:
from Denis review:

> Section 7.5 is called: "Non-linkability and data minimization"
> 
> Its first sentence is as follows:
> 
>    The verifier MUST NOT be able to infer information about data or
>    subjects not present in the presentation.
> 
> This sentence is not understandable and should be rewritten. This section should distinguish between two properties:
> "unlinkability towards a single verifier" and
> "unlinkability between different verifiers".
> One-time-use digital credentials, correctly configured and managed, are able to fulfil these two properties.
> 
> In addition, it should be observed that this section is placed under a section 7 called "Normative Requirements" which is fine.
> However, it should be indicated that, when the user accepts to disclose a subset of its attributes that allows the verifier to fully identify him,
> this specific requirement does not apply.

issues.title: Adjust selective disclosure definition
issues.author: brentzundel
issues.body:
from Denis review:

> Section 7.2 is called: "Selective Disclosure". The text states:
> 
>    A conformant implementation SHOULD identify a format for representing
>    digital credentials that make it possible for the subject to select a
>    subset of the data present in the credential for inclusion in a
>    presentation proof.
> 
> Editorial: It would be more adequate to speak about a "subset of the attributes" rather than a "subset of the data".

issues.title: Should the architecture call out trusted displays and TEEs?
issues.author: brentzundel
issues.body:
from Denis review:

> Section 7.1 is called: "Subject control". The usual term is called "User Control". There is much more to say about "Subject control".
> 
> There needs to be a protocol that has not been identified that should take place between the verifier and the User Interface managed by the digital credential manager.
> Ideally, the TUI (Trusted User Interface) managed by the TEE (Trusted Execution Environment) and the TA in charge of the management of the digital credentials should be used.
> 
> The scenario is as follows:
> (1) The subject makes a call to a verifier/relying party.
> (2) In its response, the verifier indicates a list of digital credential issuers and for each one, which types of attributes are requested, while in some case, it will indicate which values are requested.
>       Unless the following information is already available using at some metadata endpoint , for each digital credential issuer, the issuing policy(ies) of the digital credential issuer,
>       the credential format or even a profile of the digital credential shall also be indicated.
> (3) The information is transmitted to the TA.
> (4) The same information is then displayed to the subject using a TUI of the TA. In this way, the subject can be confident that, if it gives its approval,
>       what it sees on the screen will be enforced by the TA.
> This scenario mandates the transmission of machine processable data that will be displayed in the same fashion by all the digital credential managers.
> Note that this protocol is not currently being standardized by any SDO.

comments.author: brentzundel
comments.body:
Also from Denis review:

> Section 3.2 contains the following definition:
> 
>    *  A credential store is a passive repository for securely storing
>       credentials.  It supports the presentation mediator by providing
>       access to stored credentials without performing active operations.
> 
> A credential store is an internal component of a digital credential manager that stores digital credentials that are composed of several parts:
> a set of attributes about a credential subject and private cryptographic information. This definition should be removed.

> Section 5.4  is called: "Credential Store".
> 
> 5.4.  Credential Store
> 
>    The credential store is a passive repository where credentials are
>    securely stored.  Its primary function is to provide the presentation
>    mediator with access to the credentials it needs to generate
>    presentation proofs.  By separating storage from active mediation,
>    the architecture enhances modularity and allows credential stores to
>    be managed independently from presentation logic.
> 
> The credential store cannot be separated from the cryptographic engine used to create presentation proofs.
> It is recalled that the goal of the charter mentions:
> Privacy and security considerations related to the use of confidential computing, remote attestation, trusted execution environments (TEE),
> and hardware security modules (HSM) on digital credentials will be developed in coordination with relevant IETF WGs (e.g., TEEP) and
> incorporate feedback from experts on the mailing list.
> The concept of "credential store" should be removed and replaced by the concept of TA (Trusted Application) running in a TEE (Trusted Execution Environment).

issues.title: 'Presentation Flows' -> 'Credential Flows'
issues.author: brentzundel
issues.body:
The architecture is about more than just presentation

from Denis review:

> Section 6 is called: "Presentation Flows". It states:
>    Credential presentation flows describe how information from
>    credentials are transmitted from the mediator to the verifier.
> The architecture is omitting to describe the flows that are necessary to before presenting a presentation proof, whereas it should to it.

issues.title: Remove or use 'verifier service'
issues.author: brentzundel
issues.body:
from Denis review:

> The term "Verifier service" is defined in Section 3 as:
> 
>    Verifier service:  The underlying platform or infrastructure service
>       which enables a Verifier to validate a verifiable digital
>       credential.
> 
> However, the term is used nowhere else in this document. This definition should be removed.

issues.title: remove or use 'credential manager'
issues.author: brentzundel
issues.body:
from Denis review:

> The term "credential manager" is defined in Section 3 as:
> 
>    Credential manager:  An application, hardware device, or service
>       which securely stores, organizes, manages, and enables
>       presentation of credentials.  Digital wallets, password managers,
>       and passkeys managers are examples of credential managers.
> 
> Currently, this term not used anywhere else in the main body of the document.
> 
> It is proposed to replace this term by the following term and definition:
> Digital credential manager: An application supported by an hardware device which securely stores, manages digital credentials
> and derives from them presentation proofs that can then be transmitted to a verifier, after the consent of the credential subject.

issues.title: consider merging 'credential manager' and 'presentation mediator'
issues.author: brentzundel
issues.body:
from Denis review:

> The current abstract is:
> 
>    Abstract
> 
>    This document defines a reference architecture for direct
>    presentation flows of digital credentials.  The architecture
>    introduces the concept of a presentation mediator as the active
>    component responsible for managing, presenting, and selectively
>    disclosing credentials while preserving a set of security and privacy
>    promises that will also be defined.
> 
> The term "presentation mediator" which is present in the abstract, is defined in Clause 3.2 as:
> 
>    *  A presentation mediator is an active software component that
>       manages the presentation of credentials to the verifier on behalf
>       of the credential subject.
> 
> On page 9, the text states:
> 
>    (...) the presentation mediator is responsible
>    for orchestrating interactions with verifiers, performing
>    cryptographic operations, and generating presentation proofs.
> 
> This is only one part of a role that is necessary to support in the architecture. The same entity shall also be responsible for orchestrating interactions with issuers.
> The next sentence adds to the confusion, since the mediator now interacts with issuers and a "presenter" interacts with verifiers.
> 
>    The mediator is used by the subject to communicate with issuers and
>    by the presenter to communicate with verifiers. 
> 
> Rather than using the term "presentation mediator", the term "digital credential manager" is proposed.
> See a definition of this term in the comment numbered 5.
> 
> All this text will need to be revised in depth. This means that the abstract should also be revised in depth.

issues.title: Improve security considerations
issues.author: brentzundel
issues.body:
from Rohan's review:

> I'm also going to point out that the Security Considerations section is just one paragraph. [...] it would be nice to have something with more detail (at least as an outline) in the next version of the document before having to deal with WG consensus. 

from Denis review:

> Section 9 is called: "Security Considerations". This section is quite short as it only includes two sentences:
> 
>    One of the main security considerations of a direct presentation
>    credential architecture is how to establish the transactional trust
>    between both the entities (mediators, issuers and verifiers) as well
>    as the technical trust necessary for the cryptographic binding
>    between the digital credentials and their associated presentation.
>    Digital credentials are sometimes long-lived which also raises the
>    issue of revocation with its associated security requirements.
> 
> There is a lot more to say in this section. In addition to commonly known security issues (which are missing), there are two issues specific to the use of
> digital credentials when both selective disclosure and the unlinkability property towards a single verifier are required. Text about these issues is proposed below:
> 
> User collaborative attacks
> 
> When both selective disclosure and the unlinkability property towards a single verifier are both supported, collaborative attacks between individuals
> need to be taken into consideration.
> 
> If two individuals accept to collaborate, whatever kind of cryptography is used, whatever kind of protocol is used, a software-only solution will be unable
> to prevent the transfer of an attribute of an individual that possesses it, to another individual that does not possess it.
> 
> The verifier needs to know the characteristics of the application and of the hardware device supporting the application used by the individual to perform
> the access (without being able to uniquely identify the device or the application). These characteristics are present in a digital wallet attestation.
> 
> Once these characteristics are verified at the time of a digital credential request by the digital credential issuer, they can be included into the digital credential.
> In this way, the verifier will be able to know them. It will be up to the verifier to decide whether these characteristics are adequate according to the context of use.
> 
> In practice, the private cryptographic information shall be stored into the secure storage of the TEE and shall only be used by the right TA.
> 
> However, while necessary, this condition is insufficient. The private cryptographic information shall only be used by the right UA.
> This means that the TA shall only accept calls from authorized UAs.
> 
> It should be noticed that this approach is only effective during a time-limited session with a verifier.
> 
> Cross-device authorization flows
> 
> The IETF draft draft-ietf-oauth-cross-device-security-15 explores the best current practices:"Cross-Device Flows: Security Best Current Practice". Section 4.3.10 "Out of Scope“ indicates:
> For other attacks, where the user is willingly colluding with the attacker, the threat model, security implications and potential mitigations are very different”.
> When both selective disclosure and the unlinkability property towards a single verifier are both supported, collaborative attacks between individuals
> need to be taken into consideration and this IETF draft does not and will not provide solutions.
> 
> At the moment, it does not seem possible to fully defeat collaborative attacks, but it looks possible to mitigate them.
> 
> A first step, as currently recommended in the IETF draft, is to mandate a proximity mode of connection between the two devices, such as Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE),
> Near Field Communications (NFC) or Ultra Wideband (UWB). This means that the colluding individuals must be physically close together.
> 
> A second step will be needed to make sure that both devices are owned by the same person. It is anticipated that biometric controls like face recognition can be used,
> but such controls are not 100 % bullet proof and, in some cases, they can be circumvented. In this area, further investigations will be needed.

issues.title: clarify document aims
issues.author: brentzundel
issues.body:
from Rohan's review:

> What kind of document is this: The document doesn't seem sure if it is a framework, an architecture, a requirements document, or the first part of a protocol document. The only normative statements are in a section on requirements (Section 7); they are very opinionated, pretty human-credential centric, and very web-centric. If it is an architecture, we need to ditch Section 7 and refactor Section 8.

issues.title: consider more, smaller diagrams
issues.author: brentzundel
issues.body:
from @martinthomson 

I know this is a difficult limitation, but RFCs have a somewhat hard column limit that can make super-large sequence diagrams impossible to render.  You've exceeded expectations here with a diagram that is probably more than 2x the width available.

My experience is that smaller sequence diagrams are easier to understand.  Breaking larger and more complex interactions down into units can be easier to digest and can help build a more accurate picture of interactions.  Many of these larger multi-party exchanges are composed of smaller, discrete interactions that can be more clearly explained in terms of two or three parties.  Consider that approach.
